query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Co‐free equiatomic FeNiCrMn, the dynamic deformation behavior is governed primarily by dislocation glide through a landscape of composition‐induced solid-solution obstacles. At cryogenic temperatures, reduced phonon drag permits dislocation inertial effects that intensify the observed increase in CRSS, while at high temperatures enhanced atomic mobility leads to dynamic solute pinning (akin to a Cottrell-type effect) by diffusible Mn and Fe atoms. This mechanism, arising solely from local lattice distortions (due to atomic size mismatches among Fe, Ni, Cr, and Mn) without Co, governs the observed strength–ductility balance across temperature and strain-rate regimes.
generation.material_initial_state: Solidified, homogenized, equiatomic, single-phase FCC FeNiCrMn specimens produced via casting and controlled solidification followed by homogenization heat treatment; the microstructure is free of second phases and pre-existing defects are minimized.
generation.intervention: Perform compression tests on single-crystal or well-textured polycrystalline FeNiCrMn specimens oriented along a defined slip direction (e.g., [1̄23]) over a broad temperature range (from cryogenic ~10 K up to ~1073 K) at a constant engineering strain rate, with additional strain-rate jump tests at select temperatures. Complement mechanical testing with dislocation analysis via TEM to assess the slip morphology, and compare activation parameters with those predicted for solute-pinning and inertial regimes.
generation.conditions: Compression experiments from ~10 K to ~1073 K at an engineering strain rate of approximately 1×10^-4 s^-1; additional strain-rate jump tests spanning 1×10^-4 to 1×10^-2 s^-1 during early plastic deformation (~10% strain) to capture changes in apparent activation volume and inertial effects. Tests are done on specimens confirmed to be single-phase FCC by XRD and electron backscatter diffraction.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions arising from atomic size mismatches among Fe, Ni, Cr, and Mn atoms create a heterogeneous dislocation glide-resistance landscape. This mediator controls both the magnitude of the thermal activation barriers at low temperatures and the extent of dynamic solute pinning at high temperatures.
generation.mechanism: At cryogenic temperatures, thermal activation dominates dislocation motion, but a reduction in phonon damping allows dislocation inertial effects to play a significant role, resulting in a steep increase in CRSS. In contrast, at elevated temperatures, the increased diffusivity of Mn and Fe atoms leads to the formation and dynamic breaking of short-range solute atmospheres that transiently pin dislocations, yielding serrated flow behavior (a Portevin–Le Chatelier-type effect) and a modest CRSS increase relative to an intermediate-temperature baseline.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to room-temperature deformation, tests at cryogenic temperatures should show a significant rise in CRSS that levels off at very low temperatures when inertial effects become dominant. Conversely, at high temperatures (in the diffusion-active regime), there should be a modest CRSS increment along with observable serrated stress-strain responses indicative of dynamic solute pinning. These trends should correlate with measurable microstructural features (e.g., slip band patterns and local dislocation arrangements) captured by TEM.
generation.baseline: The room-temperature CRSS and deformation behavior serve as the baseline, with deviations at low and high temperatures attributed to the respective activation of inertial effects and dynamic solute pinning.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to equiatomic, single-phase FCC FeNiCrMn produced under controlled solidification and homogenization conditions. It is valid over the temperature range where the phase remains FCC and where diffusion is either negligible (cryogenic) or moderately active (approaching 1073 K), with strain rates sufficiently low to resolve thermally activated and inertial regimes.
generation.uncertainty: While the role of local lattice distortions in controlling dislocation motion is supported by analogous results in related HEAs, the quantitative contributions of dislocation inertia versus solute pinning in a Co-free system remain to be precisely determined, particularly given potential differences in atomic mobility and binding energies compared to Co-containing alloys.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a series of temperature- and strain-rate-dependent compression tests on FeNiCrMn specimens to measure the CRSS using a 0.2% offset method, supported by TEM analyses of dislocation configurations before and after deformation. Identify inertial effects from strain-rate jump tests at cryogenic temperatures by monitoring changes in apparent activation volume. At high temperatures, record any serrated flow behavior and compare CRSS increments against the intermediate-temperature baseline. Additionally, correlate mechanical response with microstructural signatures of dynamic solute pinning.
measurements: Temperature-dependent CRSS from 0.2% offset yield strength measurements
Strain-rate jump tests to capture changes in activation volume and inertial onset at cryogenic temperatures
Observation of serrated stress-strain curves indicative of dynamic solute pinning at elevated temperatures
TEM imaging of dislocation structures and slip-band characteristics at selected temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the CRSS trends do not show a substantial rise at cryogenic temperatures with a leveling-off effect at very low temperatures, or if no serrated flow behavior is observed at high temperatures (with CRSS failing to show the predicted modest increment compared to the room-temperature baseline), then the proposed mechanism of dislocation glide mediated by local lattice distortions—with distinct inertial and solute-pinning regimes—is rejected.
